title: The Dirt That Kept Doing Chemistry
hook: Sterilized soil with nothing alive in it kept running lifelike chemical reactions for six years — a clue pointing toward a 'metabolism-first' origin of life.
key_points: Researchers report lifelike biochemistry unfolding in sterilized soil for six years.
The reactions ran with no living organisms present to drive them.
It supports a 'metabolism-first' view: chemical cycles came before genes or cells.
Contrasts with ideas that a self-copying molecule like RNA came first.
content_html: How did plain chemistry on early Earth cross the line into life? One long-debated answer is "metabolism-first": the idea that self-sustaining networks of chemical reactions came first, before genes or cells, and life's machinery assembled around them. A report in Quanta Magazine describes evidence that fits this view — lifelike biochemistry that kept unfolding in sterilized soil for six years, with nothing alive present to drive it.
extra_html: That a sample scrubbed of living organisms could keep running complex, lifelike reactions on its own is the striking part. It suggests the raw chemistry of a place like soil can sustain the kind of ongoing reaction cycles that a metabolism-first origin would require — no genetic molecule needed to get started. This contrasts with the popular "RNA world" idea, which puts a self-copying molecule at the very beginning and lets metabolism follow. Origin-of-life research is far from settled, and a single observation doesn't crown a winner, but Quanta frames this as a notable point in favor of chemistry, rather than heredity, coming first.

related.title: How Life Began
related.hook: Before the first living thing, there was only chemistry. Abiogenesis is the idea — and active research — into how plain molecules on early Earth crossed the line into life.

flashcards.prompt: What does a 'metabolism-first' theory of life's origin propose?
flashcards.back_html: That self-sustaining chemical reaction cycles came first — before genes, copying molecules, or cells — and life's machinery built up from there.

flashcards.prompt: How does 'metabolism-first' differ from the RNA-world idea?

choices.text: It puts chemical cycles before a self-copying molecule, not after
It claims life never needed any chemistry
It says DNA appeared before any reactions

flashcards.explanation_html: The RNA-world view starts with a self-copying molecule; metabolism-first starts with self-sustaining reaction networks that genes joined later.
